newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Two held for attack on Iranian centre in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Two held for attack on Iranian centre in Pakistan.

text.p: Pakistani police said on Friday they had arrested two Sunni Moslem militants suspected of attacking an Iranian cultural centre in the city of Multan.

Ahmed Mubarak, superintendent of police in Multan, told Reuters that 10 other suspects were being sought in connection with Thursday's assault, which killed eight people, including the centre's Iranian director Muhammad Ali Rahimi.
He said the two detained so far were thought to be members of the Lashkar-i-Jhangvi group, linked to the militant Sunni Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) organisation.
Police had also seized 13 rocket launchers, three assault rifles, five hand grenades and other weapons and ammunition, along with Lashkar-i-Jhangvi literature, he said.

Gunmen burst into the Iranian cultural centre on Thursday and shot dead eight people, including Rahimi, whose body was flown back to Tehran on Friday, accompanied by his family and Mushahid Hussain, an aide to new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.
Sharif frequently criticised what he said was the failure of the ousted government of Benazir Bhutto to defuse sectarian violence that cost at least 170 lives in Pakistan last year.
Police used tear gas and baton-charges against Shi'ite Moslem demonstrators before funeral prayers for five of the victims, causing dozens of minor injuries, but no deaths.
Local authorities had earlier called out troops after Shi'ite protesters began chanting anti-American slogans and burning tyres on main roads in the city in Punjab province.
Police detained at least a dozen people during the trouble, the latest upsurge of sectarian unrest involving rival militants among Pakistan's majority Sunnis and minority Shi'ites.
The Iranian consulate-general in the Punjab capital Lahore accused "anti-Islamic agents of world imperialism" of carrying out Thursday's shooting, which Shi'ite leaders have blamed on the SSP.
Allama Sajid Naqvi, leader of the Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) group, said the attack was part of a conspiracy by anti-Islamic forces opposed to Pakistani-Iranian cooperation.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman said Pakistan would not let anyone disrupt its ties with Iran. "Whatever the motivations of the perpetrators, we will never allow anyone to disrupt our time-tested and fraternal relations with Iran," he said.
On January 19, SSP supporters burned the Iranian cultural centre in Lahore a day after a bomb blast there killed their leader Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi and 25 other people.
SSP followers blamed Shi'ite militants for the bombing. SSP deputy leader Azam Tariq was among about 90 wounded.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati is expected to visit Pakistan next week to deliver invitations for an Islamic summit conference to be held in Tehran in December.
Shi'ite-majority Iran has in the past urged Pakistan to protect Shi'ites from attacks by what it calls terrorists.
